newsitem.title: USA: House panel backs defense bill with B-2 bombers.
newsitem.headline: House panel backs defense bill with B-2 bombers.

text.p: A House subcommittee Thursday completed work on a $248 billion defense spending bill, which included more money for B-2 bombers and some other weapons than the Clinton administration had sought.

The defense spending bill for fiscal 1998 passed the House Appropriations National Security subcommittee on a voice vote, partly because many of the tougher issues were settled under the bipartisan budget pact between Congress and the White House.

Rep. Bill Young, a Florida Republican who heads the House subcommittee, said the panel appropriated $4.3 billion more than President Clinton's budget requested for defense. But for the current fiscal year they appropriated $9.5 billion more than the budget request.
Meanwhile, the Senate continued work on a separate defense authorization bill, which it hoped to complete Friday.

In votes on amendments Thursday, the Senate opposed re-imposing a requirement for licenses to export supercomputers to nations such as China and Russia, and defeated an attempt to soften the ban on abortions in overseas military hospitals for women in the armed forces.

Defense Secretary William Cohen was "certainly disappointed" at a 2-to-1 vote in the Senate Wednesday night to delay until at least the year 2001 closing more military bases, Pentagon spokesman Capt. Michael Doubleday said Thursday. The Pentagon sought another round of closures to get rid of costly facilities no longer needed after the Cold War.
The House panel voted to include $1.3 billion to restore the environment around bases that had been shut down in earlier rounds of base closings.

Probably the most controversial item in the House defense appropriations bill would add $331 million more than requested for the B-2 bomber program. It would add nine more of the radar-evading stealth bombers, which Cohen has called unnecessary and expensive but Young labeled a needed "deterrent to any future Saddam Husseins."
Young said the panel members realized the additional B-2 planes would require even more money in fiscal 1999, but said the panel members "made a commitment to follow through."
In other cases where the panel went beyond administration budget requests, it was based on requests from branches of the military and "not something we dreamed up," he said.
The spending bill calls for $3.68 billion for the Ballistic Missile Defense Organization, $707 million more than the Clinton budget request.
Additional expenditures include $23 million for recruiting soldiers to the all-volunteer service, and roughly $800 million for army helicopters and army vehicles.

As expected, the panel authorized a 2.8 percent pay increase for military personnel, and it stuck with earlier House bills that cut off funds for U.S. combat troops in Bosnia after June 30 of next year.
